parent.title: Pure React 19 SPA or a .NET 10 BFF? A decision framework for an internal admin console

siblings.title: In-memory tokens vs cookie-backed BFF sessions under XSS: what each architecture actually buys you
siblings.summary: httpOnly cookies do not stop XSS — they convert silent token exfiltration into loud, tab-bound session riding. That's a real but bounded win; CSP + Trusted Types is the actual mitigation.

siblings.title: Does the IETF browser-based-apps BCP apply to an internal admin console?
siblings.summary: The BCP names "business applications" in its strongest recommendation, so an internal console is in scope — but the ranking is a security/simplicity trade-off, not a normative MUST.

siblings.title: Refresh tokens and silent renew in a browser SPA (2026)
siblings.summary: Iframe silent renew is dead cross-site but alive same-site; refresh-token rotation works on both stacks, DPoP only really works on Keycloak, and TanStack Query needs a single-flight mutex either way.

siblings.title: What a BFF costs you every day: OpenAPI codegen and the local dev loop
siblings.summary: A path-preserving BFF leaves OpenAPI codegen essentially untouched — the real daily cost is one extra process, a Vite proxy config, and losing Swagger UI 'Try it out'.

siblings.title: BFF options in .NET 10: Duende.BFF, YARP, or hand-rolled
siblings.summary: If you build a BFF, the realistic .NET 10 choice is YARP + AddOpenIdConnect + the free Apache-2.0 Duende.AccessTokenManagement (~250 LOC you own), or Duende.BFF if you qualify for its free Community Edition; Duende.BFF's paid entry point is $5,750/yr.

sources.title: Duende — The BFF Pattern (Backend For Frontend)
sources.claim: The BFF proxies API calls so the SPA makes same-origin requests (CORS disappears), and CSRF is defended by SameSite cookies plus a required custom header.

sources.title: Duende BFF docs — Remote APIs
sources.claim: The BFF authenticates the frontend with a cookie, obtains the access token and forwards it to the remote API — so the remote API keeps its bearer-token auth scheme; the frontend must send a custom anti-forgery header.

sources.title: Curity — Token Handler: the SPA's new BFF
sources.claim: The token handler / BFF pattern requires minimal changes to existing APIs because they keep receiving bearer tokens; the SPA's security code is simplified.

sources.title: Duende BFF docs — Local APIs
sources.claim: BFF-local (embedded) endpoints are cookie-authenticated with an anti-forgery header and suit only single-consumer scenarios — logic placed there is not reachable by other clients.

sources.title: Tim Deschryver — Consuming a Duende BFF with Angular
sources.claim: Migrating an SPA to a BFF deletes token storage, refresh/silent-renew and the OIDC JS dependency; the CSRF interceptor is simpler than the previous bearer-token interceptor; login becomes a plain link to /bff/login.

sources.title: Duende BFF docs — Session management endpoints
sources.claim: The BFF exposes management endpoints under /bff for login, logout and querying the current user.

sources.title: Duende BFF docs — Troubleshooting
sources.claim: The common BFF failure modes are silent: UseBff() after UseAuthorization() disables anti-forgery with no error, a YARP metadata typo silently drops the token, BFF API endpoints return 401 instead of a redirect, and CORS errors mean the frontend is not same-origin with the BFF.

sources.title: Duende BFF docs — Server-side sessions
sources.claim: Without server-side sessions the access and refresh tokens live in the protected session cookie; server-side sessions require a store (an EF implementation is provided) and keep the cookie small.

sources.title: Duende — ASP.NET Core cookie size limits
sources.claim: Large claim sets push the ASP.NET Core auth cookie past the browser's 4KB limit; chunking masks it until it causes failures.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — Data Protection key storage providers
sources.claim: Multi-instance cookie auth requires a shared Data Protection key ring (Redis, Azure Blob, Key Vault or SQL) so cookies encrypted by one instance can be read by another.

sources.title: Duende — Multi-instance ASP.NET Core deployment with .NET 10
sources.claim: Deploying an ASP.NET Core cookie-based app across multiple instances requires pointing every instance at a shared key store with the same application name.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — Backends for Frontends pattern
sources.claim: Microsoft's BFF guidance lists the costs — operational overhead per extra service, an extra network hop, and probable code duplication — and says the pattern is unsuitable when only one interface interacts with the backend.

sources.title: dev.to — Backend for Frontend (BFF) in 2025: still relevant or outdated?
sources.claim: Community opinion (2024-25 Reddit/HN threads, summarised) splits on the API-shaping BFF: valuable at multi-client scale, overkill for a single-client startup.

sources.title: Duende Support #972 — WebSockets rejected by BFF anti-forgery
sources.claim: SignalR WebSocket and SSE transports fail through the Duende BFF forwarder because the WebSocket handshake cannot carry the required X-CSRF header; it falls back to long-polling.

sources.title: Duende Support #762 — SignalR support for BFF
sources.claim: Native SignalR hub support through the BFF was an open feature request rather than a shipped capability.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — ASP.NET Core authentication overview
sources.claim: ASP.NET Core can register cookie and JWT bearer handlers side by side and require any one of multiple schemes, so one API can serve both browser and bearer clients.

sources.title: Vite — Server Options (proxy)
sources.claim: Vite's dev server can proxy path prefixes such as /api and /bff to a backend, which is how a relative-path SPA runs against a BFF locally.

sources.title: Duende — Licensing
sources.claim: Duende BFF is free for companies under $1M annual revenue and requires a paid licence above that threshold.

sources.title: Duende — BFF v4: multi-frontend, OpenTelemetry, simplified security
sources.claim: Duende BFF v4 hosts multiple frontends in a single BFF host, removing the one-BFF-per-SPA operational sprawl.

sources.title: thoughtbot — One-way vs two-way door decisions
sources.claim: One-way-door decisions are costly to reverse and warrant deliberation; two-way-door decisions should be made fast and iterated on.

sources.title: Alpha Hydrae — Displaying an image protected by header-based authentication
sources.claim: HTML elements like and cannot send an Authorization header, so a bearer-token SPA needs fetch+blob workarounds for protected images and downloads — workarounds a cookie-based BFF makes unnecessary.

sources.title: oidc-spa docs — The JWT of the access token
sources.claim: The access token is meant to be opaque to the client; decoding it in frontend code to read claims is discouraged.

sources.title: OneUptime — Keycloak client creation
sources.claim: In Keycloak a SPA is configured with Client authentication OFF (public client) while a server-side web app has Client authentication ON (confidential client) — the BFF switch is a toggle plus new redirect URIs.

sources.title: Wrapt — Using Duende BFF with React
sources.claim: Wiring a React SPA to a Duende BFF is a small amount of code: a claims hook calling /bff/user with an X-CSRF header, login/logout links, and API routes forwarded via MapRemoteBffApiEndpoint.

sources.title: Duende — The cookie apocalypse already happened
sources.claim: Third-party cookie deprecation is complete across major browsers, so a cookie-based BFF must be deployed same-site with the SPA.
